column2: Famous for his progressive ideas on music in schools and for his Concord Summer School of Music, Surette at first comes often enough to be considered a visiting teacher, then accepts a post in 1937. His musical influence is eclipsed by his literary interests: he read Blake aloud constantly, and everyone began reading Blake. Consequences: music education flourishes in the curriculum; a vogue for Blake

The article “Fundamentalism and the Higher Learning,” replying to Hutchins's program (University of Chicago, the great classic texts, truth the same everywhere): Rice formulates there his clearest philosophy — education as learning a way of doing, not acquiring a stock of ideas; knowing is not enough. Hutchins, The Higher Learning in America, 1936; article pp. 587-588, 595 Consequences: a public definition of BMC's philosophy

The eight students do not return; Zeuch and King find other posts during the summer, bringing to five the number of faculty members who did not come back. The year begins with 55 students enrolled. 55 students enrolled; five faculty departures Consequences: An apparent clearing of the air

While Nell is making long stays in Sullivan (Indiana) after her mother's death, Rice falls in love with a young student, met during the fall ritual of visiting back and forth among the students' studies. He describes it as a sudden spasm caused by his unhappy marriage. Rumors; no one knows whether the relationship was physical. It will later emerge that the young woman was more interested in another student. A drink shared in the studies; earlier rumors about Rice with a drama teacher at the New Jersey College for Women and a secretary in Henry Allen Moe's office Consequences: Nell catches Rice in the act; community fury after Christmas

His parents visit Frank in Chapel Hill and take him to dinner at the Carolina Inn. Rice leaves the table for the restroom; Nell, her face twisted with anger (like a furious cat), whispers to her son: “I caught him at it. I saw him with her.” Frank gets up, walks to his room, weeps on his bed, then keeps silent toward his parents for weeks. Dinner at the Carolina Inn, Chapel Hill's chic restaurant Consequences: A lasting family wound; community conflict

A first public success: his design for the Hall of Pharmacy at the 1939 New York World's Fair is accepted, then turned into a full-size painting by professional muralists. Consequences: A short-lived success: struck off the WPA rolls.
De Kooning moves into a new loft; there his dialogue with Picasso and Gorky leads to a series of self-portraits from 1938. He meets Franz Kline and Barnett Newman toward the end of the 1930s.

Receives a commission for a mural in the Hall of Pharmacy at the 1939 New York World's Fair (executed by professional muralists); meets Philip Guston, Barnett Newman, and the art student Elaine Fried, who becomes his student. Consequences: The start of the relationship with his future wife and student

The AAA group, founded in 1937 in reaction to social realism and inspired by De Stijl, does not count de Kooning among its members: he was with them in spirit, but he disapproved of their narrowness, of their telling him not to do something. Quotation: “I disagreed with their narrowness, their telling me not to do something” Consequences: Independence between figuration and abstraction
Herbert Bayer falls out of favor with the German government only in 1937, after working on its propaganda exhibitions. Consequences: Precedes his departure for the United States
Despite his propaganda work, Bayer loses the favor of the German government — he has a Jewish wife and does not support Nazi policy. Consequences: A prelude to his departure for the United States.

Gropius, the first one invited for the post, recommends him; he teaches at the Harvard Graduate School of Design and in 1938 becomes head of the architecture department. Consequences: Bauhaus exhibitions multiply at MoMA and elsewhere; the Bauhaus enters the bloodstream of American culture

Together with Marcel Breuer, the Gropiuses emigrate so that Walter can teach at Harvard's Graduate School of Design. An American citizen in 1944; founds The Architects Collaborative (TAC) in 1945; dies in 1969 at 86, having spread his architectural vision around the world — sometimes with hubris (the Pan Am Building). TAC founded 1945; Pan Am Building

The Nazis seize 102 Klees from German museums in 1937 and include 17 in the “Entartete Kunst” exhibition in Munich; the catalog compares his paintings to the work of institutionalized schizophrenics and sees “confusion” in them. 102 works seized, 17 shown

The Third Reich confiscates 102 Klees from German museums and shows 17 of them in the “Entartete Kunst” exhibition in Munich; the catalog compares his paintings to the work of hospitalized schizophrenics and sees in them proof of a psychologically unstable character. 102 works seized; 17 shown in Munich Consequences: Klee branded the most degenerate of the degenerate artists
An early first exhibition of watercolors of the Maine coast; he then moves on to tempera and has alternated between the two mediums ever since.

After the long Christmas vacation, Zeuch formally petitions the Board to reconsider its action against Knickerbocker and Goldenson; the petition is rejected. A “bone” thrown to Goldenson: permission to resign, as he claimed he had wanted Consequences: The dissidents turn to questions of governance

Around midwinter, the affair begins. Rice, walking with a student, explains that he knows Alice a little better because she needs to be “brought out,” to feel important, to “blossom” — the posture of a kindly father. At an evening of skits, Alice, in a papier-mâché costume that makes her body tiny and her head enormous, parodies an opera singer; everyone is amused except Rice, who is jealous. A papier-mâché costume, an enormous head Consequences: Rice, after the power struggle, is about to “rock the community” with a love affair

Meyer concludes his indictment of the ancient evil of advertising: he has dealt with only one aspect (unproductive effort, the creation of inordinate desires, the habit of advertising); the billboards, so insulting and so nervous, did not survive; so today they are tearing down these billboards. No applause: there is nothing to rejoice over. a billboard draped in a lemon-yellow curtain; Meyer sits back down among the audience Consequences: announces the demolition

Around 5 p.m., tea and cakes are handed out; three carpenters explain the technique: the supports at the back sawed through, left standing on a few props, notches cut in the front posts as when felling pines; Tony pushes with all his weight, two others pull the props away with ropes; the billboard collapses with a crack and a dull “bunnnnng,” a cloud of dust, revealing the field of grass and meadowflowers. The right-hand billboard, draped in lemon yellow, is kept. Tony's cigar wrapped in paper, tucked into his breast pocket, relit later; the countdown One—two—and three!; children gone around behind to watch Consequences: the field restored; one billboard kept to be rededicated

Behind a burgundy curtain held by two young carpenters on ladders: a young linden with heart-shaped leaves and a few cream-colored flowers in the sunlight. Dido explains: what appears behind a curtain or in a frame, one considers more calmly, in itself. Astonishment, almost disappointment at first, then the understanding that the leaves and petals are the organs of the invisible roots; the tree had grown up hidden behind a fence. Furious applause for three or four minutes; Dido suggests displaying a single tree in the middle of a theater stage; Meyer objects that the tree would be less beautiful away from its meadow; Dido disagrees. The audience hopes for a dialectical joust, which does not take place. burgundy curtain, lemon-yellow curtain, ladders, heart-shaped leaves, cream-colored flowers Consequences: the linden becomes one of the traditions of the Ninth of May

Harry, a baseball glove on his wrist, pulls a crumpled sheet from his hip pocket and reads in a firm voice a poem composed that day about the meadowflowers growing softly in the tall grass amid the noise of the ball game. No applause (boys are not applauded; everyone is out of the habit of advertising), except from the children. Dido draws him close and murmurs: “It is true, it is true!—the meadowflowers grow softly in the knee-deep grass”; the boy blushes to his ears and refuses to repeat what was said. a fielder's glove hanging from his wrist; a crumpled sheet from his hip pocket; whispered remarks from the other boys Consequences: the reading of this poem becomes customary on the Ninth of May

A quartet that has come more than a hundred miles plays Beethoven's Quartet in B-flat, Op. 130. Principles established by Dido and followed throughout the country: never a public gathering without excellent music; one does not take the unprepared soul by surprise with complicated music — they begin with simple chords, major and minor. The children and several adults wander off for half an hour. A description of the four musicians; during the Danza alla Tedesca, Dido, haggard, thinks with horror of his wasted life and weeps; little Viola laughs and sings along with the score, Mrs. Troy smiles at her queenly. A half-minute pause before the Cavatina; Maritimus's gaze over the audience; during the Cavatina, the listeners are as if dead, eyes open but unseeing, arms in awkward positions; a very small child comes in from the field and is frightened; at the turn of the melody, tears flow. music stands set up; the tuning of the instruments, plucked notes falling into the deepening silence; Tony's cigar relit

Late afternoon, an egg-shaped sun behind the hill tinting the linen. Dido decorates the rescued billboard and proposes a principle: to post in public vehicles a poem, a mathematical theorem, or the reasoning of a beautiful physical experiment — a single act of thought worth having; but he doubts it can be extended to billboards, since souls can be too much occupied, preoccupied. The sun sets; he cannot break the silence and merely makes a gesture; two boys let go of the yellow curtain: an elegantly printed sentence and a large circle appear. Miss Campbell, the English teacher, thinks the word “describe” ill chosen. The planet Venus shines over the hill; the gathering breaks up. the setting sun tinting the linen; Venus, the Sun's afterthought Consequences: the founding of the traditions of the “May Ninth”: burgundy and lemon yellow, the linden, the reading of the poems of Dido and Walker

A satirical fable about the commodity (epigraph from Capital, Book I). Impetigo, who once bought twelve gross of scissors at wholesale, waves a two-dollar bill (reputed unlucky) at the supermarket: Alcoa has just published a full page printed in aluminum paint in the Saturday Evening Post extolling its utensils (they will wear forever, shine on the wall, no dirt in the curves); that same Tuesday, the company withdraws the line to reserve the metal for National Defense. It is not real frustration that brings him close to a nervous breakdown, but the horrors of the imagination: the motorist in the rain to whom the Texaco ad promises comfort around the next bend, when it is forbidden to sell gasoline after sunset. The economist Impetigo sees with satisfaction that advertising is refining its effects (everyone wants and absolutely needs everything) and with dread the inadequacy of private incomes. The economist's face turned white. a two-dollar bill; twelve gross of scissors; a metal pot with a “Titegrip” lid; an advertising page in aluminum paint; aluminum collected by the Boy Scouts on July 4; the saleswoman's reply: “The Boy Scouts will collect your aluminum on the Fourth of July”

In Social Frontier, Dewey reproaches Hutchins for his reliance on fixed authority: without calling him a fascist, he likens his approach to a distrust of freedom; who will decide the final truths? Rice, a friend of Dewey's, endorses this criticism. Social Frontier, III, January 1937, pp. 103-104

Forty kilometers in two hours on waterlogged roads; the driver lays stones and mattresses to get across the ruts; a bumpy arrival, forgotten at once before ruins new to them Words: Toni Fleischmann in her diary: the road is very bad, almost impassable in the heavy rains Atmosphere: Mud, rain, jolts, then wonder Stakes: The physical price of the archaeological dream

Forty kilometers in two hours on a road ruined by heavy rains; the driver steers through the mud and gets out several times with a helper to clear the way with a pickax and lay stones; the passengers arrive shaken but forget everything before ruins unlike any they had seen; the next day, switchbacks up to Monte Albán. Words: Toni Fleischmann's diary: the road is very bad, almost impassable because of the heavy rains; the ancients always built their temples in the most beautiful places. Atmosphere: Mud, effort, jolts — then wonder. Stakes: The physical price of access to the sources of art.

Zeuch: academically a dead loss, he has not improved. Mangold: does he have enough intelligence? Zeuch: he does not have enough willpower. Mangold: he drank too much this semester. Gair (a student): he has talked with him and with Leslie, his roommate; this place scares him, perhaps more than any other would. Decision: postponed. Words: “Academically, I think he is a dead loss” (Zeuch); “this place scares him” (Gair) Atmosphere: The teachers' clinical frankness about absent students Stakes: A frightened, drinking student on the verge of exclusion

Schawinsky: last term he was completely self-centered; now he does things for the group; sometimes he does nothing for days, but one cannot know whether he is not thinking. Evarts: progress, but it would be better for him to find a job — he would learn to cooperate. Weston: we are failing with a person of great ability. Albers: very talented but very one-sided; always intellectual; a harsher environment would do him good; he needs a strong reality. Verdict: better for him to go out into the world. Stakes: Talent versus community commitment

Mangold: very good work but does not speak in class; second year; should we keep her? Wunsch: what is her influence? Mangold: dead in that respect. Steinau: a dead weight. King: last year she felt like a freak, not this year; let us give her one more year. Albers: he has an image of her, the same as on the first day — and it is not a mask. French: intellectually, she should come back. Rice: a case where the College has failed; we let her live in a small circle; she is more isolated than ever; it will always be an F — for the College; what she wants most is to be liked, and no one in the world finds her important. Verdict: doubt about her return, to be told to her parents if she wants to come back; the admissions committee and the treasurer can always refuse. Words: “The most important thing for her is to be liked. The difficulty is that there is nobody in the world who thinks she is important” (Rice) Atmosphere: The awkward pity of a faculty that recognizes its own failure Stakes: An isolated student, a mirror of the community's failure

Portell: her family (Midwesterners settled in the South) and her high school have had a bad effect; her papers are very good and call for independent thought; yesterday she handed in a paper on Black people three days early — a paper that took real courage for someone from Georgia. Zeuch: the only two Southern students here feel inferior to the Northerners. Portell: she is aware of her financial situation; she must be helped. Albers: she has a mathematical understanding; he believes in her, as Portell does; she needs more time. Rice: that puts her at a mental age of about six; he disagrees with Albers and Portell — but when someone is brought here, a commitment is made; one must not give up before doing everything. Albers: her brain is better than her mouth; she is worth more than many others. Verdict: she stays. Words: “That brings her up to about six years old” (Rice) Atmosphere: A courteous clash between Rice and Albers-Portell, settled in the student's favor Stakes: Must the college honor its debt to a poor Southern student?

Alice appears in a papier-mâché costume that makes her body tiny and her head enormous, parodying an opera singer; the audience is amused — except Rice, already gnawed by jealousy. Atmosphere: General laughter, the muted anxiety of a man in love Stakes: The fatherly mentor gives himself away as a jealous lover

A country meal under the trees; Rice, in round steel-rimmed glasses, talks animatedly facing Huxley, photographed from behind in the foreground Atmosphere: Summer relaxation, trees, crisscrossing conversations Stakes: The college receives the most famous writer of its young history

His parents invite Frank to dinner. Rice goes off to the restroom; Nell leans toward her son, her face hardened like a furious cat's, and whispers her secret. Frank gets up without a word, walks to his room, falls on his bed, and weeps; his parents knock at his door, he cannot speak to them and will keep silent toward them for weeks. Words: Nell: “I caught him at it. I saw him with her.” Atmosphere: A chic restaurant, a sudden lurch into emotional violence Stakes: An intimate wound that compounds the public crisis

Tony takes up his cigar again, explains the felling technique, counts One—two—and three!, and pushes with all his weight; a crack, a dull “bunnnnng,” a cloud of dust; the field and the flowers reappear; the children behind shout “Ready!” Words: “O.K., boys— Ready? Here goes! One—two—and three!” Atmosphere: the audience starts at the crack; dust; laughter of the carpenters reappearing Stakes: a concrete and joyful victory over advertising

After the half-minute pause and Maritimus's gaze, the Cavatina begins; the audience becomes as if dead: eyes open but unseeing, bodies graceless, arms in awkward positions; a small child comes in from the field and is frightened; at the turn of the melody, tears flow, breathing becomes formal with the song Atmosphere: absolute silence, the gentle violence of the music, tears, evening light Stakes: the total aesthetic experience that holds the whole community suspended

Harry, unapplauded, stuffs his sheet into his pocket and walks away; Dido draws him close and murmurs that his line is true; the boy blushes deeply; the others ask what was said; he will not tell Words: “It is true, it is true!—the meadowflowers grow softly in the knee-deep grass” Atmosphere: hushed complicity, the child's modesty Stakes: the master's legacy to the young poet, in secret

Student discussions and community meetings in late winter and spring 1937 on how much say each person should have. Rice replies that the college is first of all an educational venture, not a community, and that he is a better judge than anyone of who should teach. Zeuch prefers to trust the whole community rather than a small group. Consequences: Eight students resign in protest

During the spring vacation of the 4th year, four students (two boys, two girls) go to Florida together. When they return, the college judges that they have not been intelligent and have risked the moral reputation of the institution, already suspected of being a center of free love. The Board of Fellows and the faculty meet several times, with the student officers taking part and those concerned summoned. Mort Steinau's diary: April 7 (the Board sits with the four), April 8 (decision that Fred and Mrs. Moellenhoff will talk to them), April 9 (student meeting on mixed groups traveling) Consequences: A provisional agreement: mixed groups do not go on vacation together; no other sanction

Huxley, who has come on his own initiative with his wife, his son, and his friend Gerald Heard, chats with everyone, asks difficult questions about the United States, is astonished at the poverty of the Deep South, praises America's extraordinary hopefulness, deplores the dictatorship of the bosses, and wonders how self-government can be carried down into industry. One evening, a round table on the limits of the novel. Heard, even more impressive to many, talks of ridding oneself of every addiction and of unlimited responsibility among the members of a true community, announces that man will soon be able to converse with trees and flowers, and says that telepathy and clairvoyance remain to be explored by the West. The general verdict: “damn nice”; one teacher has the impression of talking to Huxley by transatlantic telephone — his eyes have something to do with it

A community meeting lasting several hours: Alsberg and Coleman question Rice about flattering students, the faculty's alleged superiority, and the students' competence to choose teachers. Rice rejects the equality of opinions (“there are incompetent people here”) and offers to give up his permanent tenure; Sargent retorts that this is easy, since it remains in his power. King pleads for sharing responsibility for choosing the governing committee. The meeting ends without a conclusion. Alsberg to Rice: “I say you are crazy”; Rice: “Intelligence is not contained in barrels. If it were I would order a lot of it now.”; “less organization and more organism” Consequences: The last three months of the term remain marked by division
Mangold reports to Adamic that Knickerbocker and his cause have collapsed: when he was away for two and a half weeks, the college did not even notice.

An informal talk that turns into a discussion: the difficulty of embodying ideas without parading them, the impossibility of good characters in Dickens and Shakespeare, the cultural conventions that limit the definition of the human, Homer and Fielding as models of vital robustness. Words: All of Dickens's good people suffer from extreme infantilism; the Duke in Measure for Measure is not a human being but a symbol of Christianity; Homer: his characters broke off their grief to have supper — and then grieved again Atmosphere: Intellectual, intimate Stakes: What is left of the novel in the face of life?

Alsberg asks whether a student should never be flattered; Rice: never. Coleman: isn't flattery persuasion? Rice distinguishes according to use. Alsberg tries sarcasm: someone who persuades a majority would be undesirable; Rice: that depends. Five minutes of diversion; Coleman comes back: why does the faculty claim so much superiority? Rice answers with a question. Alsberg: “you can't say I am incompetent”; Rice: he is not in a position to choose the faculty; Alsberg: “you are crazy”; Rice, calmly: intelligence is not sold by the barrel. Sargent points to Rice's tenure; Rice offers to give it up; Sargent: that is in his power. King pleads for harmony; Rice sidesteps. Zeuch proposes trusting the whole community; Rice and Dreier maintain that some opinions are worth more. The meeting peters out without a conclusion. Words: “Yes, George, never.” / “Intelligence is not contained in barrels. If it were I would order a lot of it now.” Atmosphere: A marathon of several hours, weariness, verbal fencing, restrained irony Stakes: Should power belong to the competent or to the community?

The Fleischmanns arrive in Veracruz aboard the S.S. Orinoco, bringing the paintings and photographs left in Germany in 1933. The two couples travel nearly 6,000 miles, often in the Alberses' new two-seater car: Puebla, Tehuacán by car, then a twelve-hour train to Oaxaca; an excursion to Mitla (40 km in two hours on unpaved mud roads) and to Monte Albán the next day. Toni Fleischmann's diary: heavy rains, mud puddles, a driver laying stones and mattresses to get across the ruts; admiration for temples built in the most beautiful sites Consequences: Direct biographical (the diary) and archaeological material feeding the narrative

Siegfried and Toni Fleischmann arrive in Veracruz on the S.S. Orinoco for the second Mexican summer, bringing the paintings and photographs Josef had left in Germany in 1933. The two couples travel about 6000 miles, often in the Alberses' new two-seater car; a train from Tehuacan to Oaxaca (12 hours); an excursion to Mitla (40 km, 2 hours on muddy, broken roads, the driver and a helper repairing the way with a pickax and stones); the next day, switchbacks up to Monte Albán. S.S. Orinoco; 6000 miles (~9650 km); 12 hours by train; 40 km in 2 hours; heavy rains, mud; Toni Fleischmann's diary

Coleman reads a 24-point critique signed by eight students, all leaving for good: malicious gossip, too much emphasis on social development, a low standard of work, a puritanical morality worthy of a Baptist girls' school, an approach too intuitive and mystical, the concentration of power in the Board of Fellows, and, against Rice: intimidating students, a one-man school, an “unbalanced egoist” with an “i am god” complex. 24 points, 8 signers; Coleman claims “a considerable degree of detachment” Consequences: The eight leave the college

A new point: the college has starved Georgia (a teacher with life tenure) by cutting his salary from 1,500 to 1,300 dollars. Alsberg reveals that Zeuch had reported to them a remark Rice made the previous fall: Georgia “had to be gotten rid of,” and the sure way was to keep his salary low. Rice admits the remark but demands that Zeuch, in bed with a headache, appear; Zeuch denies having approved of Georgia's departure and says he only offered to help him find another post. Georgia's salary: $1,500 → $1,300; Mangold: “about the tensest thing that has ever happened around here” Consequences: The salary mechanisms publicly revealed

The system explained: in the first two years, salary based solely on need; from the third year on, value to the college is taken into account, the whole decided in secret by the treasurer, Dreier. The first public disclosure of amounts: Rice and Wunsch $2,100 each (1936-1937), Albers $1,700. Rice $2,100; Wunsch $2,100; Albers $1,700; Georgia $1,300

Portell shouts that he is worth as much as anyone: his salary has gone from $1,500 (1935-1936) to $1,250 (1936-1937); Albers and Wunsch have new cars, he a used one; Mrs. Rice receives $200 as dietitian, while his wife Lea, who teaches Spanish, is not paid. He lifts his chair as if to throw it out the window, controls himself, puts it down, then walks out with his arms folded like a wrestler, followed by his wife. $1,500 → $1,250; $200 to Nell Rice Consequences: Mangold speaks of an “insane and infantile” scene; Rice writes to Henry Allen Moe (Guggenheim): “never seen a grown man make a more disgraceful exhibition,” mocks Latin pride, and offers his services as an opera director

Rice reproaches Georgia for his laziness, his lack of involvement, his few students and friends, his dull and conventional teaching, his silence. Mrs. Georgia says they would agree to leave if a suitable job were found: they had stayed only out of necessity, having used up $3,000-4,000 of savings in four years. Georgia says he would leave even without a job if Rice's opinion were shared; he does not think it is. An informal vote: eight or nine against him, fewer for him. He leaves the meeting with his wife and slams the door of his office three times. Savings used up: $3,000 to $4,000; three door slams

After hours of chaos, Rice takes control again and convinces the majority that the college will come out of it stronger. A student notes in his diary that evening: “The old maestro—calmly, wisely, gave an accurate picture of the whole mix-up”; within ten minutes the community feels more united than at the start, five hours earlier. “The whole silent group sighed, smiled, and left by all the doors in the lobby.” A meeting of about five hours

While the students are moving out and carrying the furniture up to the attics, the Board receives Portell's resignation but tables it, then has it withdrawn after a talk with Rice (he will leave anyway at the end of the following year). Georgia's resignation is accepted: he agrees to resign immediately in exchange for the monetary equivalent of a year's salary, set at $3,500. $3,500 requested by Georgia; Rice judges the agreement “cheap at the price” but mocks the savings “often remarked upon” Consequences: Georgia leaves the college

King and Zeuch decide not to return, completing the rout of the anti-Rice camp. Before leaving, Zeuch leaves a five-thousand-word critique, “The State of Black Mountain College”. Consequences: Rice's power consolidated

Moellenhoff: a semester at BMC is like an Atlantic crossing in the days of sailing ships — many perils, some possible reward. Evarts (absent, relieved): “bluntness has its limits”. Howard: the public humiliation of the Georgias was “a dismal display,” but he learned “what war feels like”. Mangold: “the best year the college had had”. Steinau: whoever said pioneer life wasn't hard?

The college repays Georgia in two installments of 250 dollars and six of 500 dollars, without interest; a legal agreement is signed on June 3, 1937. Rice mentions Georgia's savings. Total $3,500; a legal agreement dated June 3, 1937

After the meeting, Georgia, told by Rice and others that his low salary reflected problems with his teaching and insufficient community involvement, resigns (accepted). Portell-Vila, furious at salaries higher than his own, also resigns, but Rice persuades him to stay. Consequences: Georgia leaves the faculty

The college buys a former 700-acre girls' camp on the shore of Lake Eden, three miles north of the Blue Ridge site, doing away with the annual lease and with storing the furniture every June. Rice is less euphoric than others. 700 acres, three miles north of the Blue Ridge site Consequences: Planning of the permanent campus begins

Coleman reads the twenty-four grievances; the matter of Georgia's salary blows the meeting apart. A student asks whether the information came from a teacher. An evasive answer. Alsberg reveals Rice's remark as reported by Zeuch. Rice demands Zeuch, who is in bed, appears, and denies it. Salaries are disclosed. Portell explodes: the others' new cars, his wife unpaid; he wrenches his chair off the floor, seems about to throw it out the window, masters himself, puts it down, and walks out with his arms folded, followed by Lea. Georgia is called into question: laziness, few friends; Mrs. Georgia pleads their poverty; an informal vote against him; he leaves, slamming his office door three times. Then Rice, in ten minutes, turns the room around: the community feels more united than before, smiles, and leaves by all the doors of the lobby. Words: Portell: he is worth as much as anyone; Rice to Moe two days later: “never seen a grown man make a more disgraceful exhibition of himself” Atmosphere: Five hours of tension, shouting, physical threat, then almost euphoric relief Stakes: Money reveals the hidden hierarchies; Rice's charisma absorbs the chaos

Anni's parents join them from June 19 to July 16. The four visit Teotihuacán, Tenayuca, Tepoztlán, Toluca, Cuernavaca, Taxco, Tlalpan, Tlaxcala, Santa Ana, Puebla, Cholula, Tehuacán, Oaxaca, Mitla, Monte Albán. Toni keeps an enthusiastic diary (the Toluca market, Monte Albán, the museum of folk art). They buy little clay heads of gods for a few cents. Toni Fleischmann's diary

A stay at Calle de Paris 23; Anni's parents present from June 19 to July 16; a grand tour; Toni scrupulously notes everything in her diary (the Toluca market, the temples of Monte Albán, the museum of folk art, clay miniatures bought for a few cents).

Rice calls children general nuisances, asserts that humans are closer to monkeys than is believed in their limited capacity to reason, and tells his audience that they would learn more from their children than by trying to teach them. The Business Men's Evangelical Clubs of North Carolina call him radical and communist; a week of angry letters and editorials appears in the Charlotte News. Charlotte News, an afternoon daily; “Rice's Talk Draws Fiery Censure,” 1937-10-26, pp. 1, 8; “Hold up Your Hands,” 1937-10-27, p. 6; “Dave Believes Everything,” 1937-10-24, p. 8 Consequences: a reputation as a provocateur throughout the state

Rice calls children general nuisances, likens human reason to that of monkeys, and advises his audience to learn from their children rather than try to teach them. The evangelical businessmen's clubs denounce him as radical and communist; a week of anger in the letters and editorials of the Charlotte News. Words: children, general nuisances; humans closer to monkeys than is believed; learn from your children Atmosphere: public scandal, an inflamed letters column Stakes: the notoriety of Rice and the college in conservative North Carolina
From November 1937, the fees at the American Artists School amount to five dollars a month. 5 dollars a month.

About three months after the start of the term, two students run off together; the community reacts calmly; the rector is more upset than anyone. Consequences: Rice's distress may reflect his own fantasies of flight (his budding affair with Alice).

At an evening of skits, Alice, dressed as an opera singer in a papier-mâché costume that shrank her body and enlarged her head, amuses everyone except Rice, who declares himself “shocked” and judges the act in detestable taste. Papier-mâché costume: a tiny body, an enormous head; a parody of an opera singer. Consequences: The faculty comes to think that it is Rice who is playing the buffoon, out of jealousy.

Alice, in a papier-mâché costume that makes her body tiny and her head enormous, parodies an opera singer; everyone laughs except Rice, who says he is “shocked” and declares that Alice is a woman, and a fine one, and that it was in detestable taste to make a buffoon of her. Words: Rice: “shocked”; Alice is “a woman and a fine one”. Atmosphere: General laughter, then unease at the rector's anger. Stakes: Rice's jealousy becomes visible to the community.

They meet at a political action meeting connected with the Artists Union, where each represents his or her school; an affair hidden from Elaine's parents. He encourages her to join the American Artists School on West 14th Street, a reincarnation of the John Reed Club's school. Consequences: Elaine changes schools; already an affair she conceals (the “knocked up” business with her father).

Jonas introduces Elaine to de Kooning in his immaculate studio; on the easel, a bald man in a loose jacket painted in ocher and olive green; Elaine is certain she is dealing with a genius A floor covered with industrial linoleum, frugally salvaged and painted battleship gray; de Kooning blond, blue-eyed, with a clear and open gaze, a compact build Consequences: Elaine confides to her sister Marjorie that she has fallen in love, although she is closely attached to Milton (Resnick)

De Kooning tells her to give up her women with eyes turned heavenward and blood running down their arms (inspired by the Spanish Civil War) in favor of spatial relationships, best taught by a still life, since master and student look at the same objects Painting: a coffeepot, a large shell, a yellow cup, an old blue cotton shirt, an army blanket; three months of effort Consequences: A discipline that later allowed her, she says, to explode into abstract painting

Elaine, Resnick, and Blumberg leave the loft at Fourth Avenue and 29th Street for a larger space First loft: $30 a month, ten dollars each; the ground floor rented out by day to an opera singer for extra income
A text in MoMA's catalog Bauhaus 1919-1928, edited by Herbert Bayer and Walter and Ise Gropius.

Fifth year: Dick Porter, a withdrawn boy who had often threatened to kill himself and was thought to be immune, shoots himself in the right temple one afternoon; Moellenhoff and the local doctor, Dr. Richardson, take him to the Biltmore Hospital in Asheville, where he dies on the operating table without regaining consciousness; he had never come to Moellenhoff for help (who, moreover, was not licensed to practice in the United States and could have helped him only informally). a bullet in the right temple; death on the operating table; a general meeting the next morning Consequences: the community in shock; a feeling of guilt

The next morning, at a general meeting, Moellenhoff declares that when a person is alone in the midst of a group, a feeling of guilt arises in the community — but that loneliness is often chosen and self-imposed.
Staging of Irwin Shaw's antimilitarist play without a stage, with sets in sections surrounding the audience — an innovation due mainly to the designer George Hendrickson.

A production “in the round” with an original score by John Evarts played by the orchestra under Allan Sly; the audience, identically masked and hooded, forms the outer circles of the performance. Identical masks and capes for the spectators. Consequences: A multimedia celebration some fifteen years before the famous Cage/Cunningham/Olson/Rauschenberg event of 1952.

Nell alternates between the role of official hostess for her brother Frank Aydelotte, president of Swarthmore, a library school in Chapel Hill, and an apprenticeship as a librarian in Asheville — which keeps her away from Black Mountain and too busy to grumble.

Hostility toward Rice subsides for a time: Portell resigns, and the new members of the staff include Peggy (Loram) and David Bailey, among Rice's oldest friends and admirers. Consequences: A modus vivendi with Dreier and Albers, relations that are “workable,” according to Mangold.

After hearing Josef Jonas declare that the two best American artists (de Kooning and Gorky) were not in the American Abstract Artists exhibition, Elaine decides to meet de Kooning; it takes her about two weeks. She knows at once that he is a genius and that she will marry him. about two weeks between the decision and the meeting Consequences: a master-student relationship, then marriage

Elaine was still Resnick's lover when she met Bill; Resnick understands that he has lost her and transfers his affection to de Kooning in a kind of hero worship: his own painting begins to resemble Bill's, and he ends up speaking with a Dutch accent. Bill marvels to friends at seeing this man still hanging around after his girlfriend has been taken from him. Resnick speaking with a Dutch accent Consequences: a lasting triangle of friendship and love

Elaine, back from Brooklyn, spends her time in Bill's studio on West Twenty-second Street; to her family, the lovers claim that Bill is teaching her drawing — which is partly true. the studio on West 22nd Street Consequences: real drawing lessons

Living on window dressing for A.S. Beck, Bill turns down an offer of 100 dollars a week to go and design windows in Philadelphia, preferring to stay poor in New York, close to art. 100 dollars a week, a lot of money at the end of the 1930s Consequences: poverty embraced in the service of painting
Albers writes: to distribute material goods is to divide them; to distribute spiritual goods is to multiply them.

Five years after her arrival, Anni Albers publishes in the Black Mountain College Bulletin this essay on working with material, in which unshaped material is the ground least subject to authority, favorable to invention and free speculation.

Gropius, coeditor of the catalog of the exhibition Bauhaus 1919-1928 at MoMA, reproduces on its last pages exercises by Albers's students at Black Mountain, displaying the teaching legacy. An exhibition organized by Bayer with the help of Gropius, Albers, and Schawinsky; pages 205-17 of the catalog.

Penley becomes the college's first farmer; with the energy of the mathematician Theodore Dreier, the farm takes shape: acres of vegetables, dozens of acres of pasture, then livestock (a dairy herd and pigs). a dairy herd, pigs Consequences: The community eats the farm's produce from 1938, even before living there (1941).

Although he had heard of the college from Stoller, an architectural photographer, it is at the 1938 Bauhaus exhibition at MoMA that Black Mountain catches his attention. The New Bauhaus and BMC were both represented there; BMC attracts him with its sliding scale of tuition. He applies to both and is accepted by both. sliding tuition scale Consequences: He chooses Black Mountain.

An interview over dinner with Xanti Schawinsky, a former Bauhaus student then teaching at BMC, in a restaurant on the Hudson, decides Stoller to choose Black Mountain. a restaurant on the Hudson River; Schawinsky described as “ever-charming” Consequences: Enrollment at BMC.

Window Picture (1921) is mounted in a portable light box, no doubt for the traveling exhibition “Bauhaus: How it Worked” (1939-40) organized by MoMA, so as to preserve the stained-glass effect Albers sought. Hirshhorn accession number 72.6 (Fensterbild).

In 1938, Window Picture (Fensterbild, Hirshhorn 72.6) is mounted in a transportable light-box frame, no doubt to preserve the stained-glass effect for the traveling exhibition Bauhaus: How it Worked (1939-40) organized by MoMA. Hirshhorn accession number 72.6; MoMA, 1939-40. Consequences: Preserves the effect of transmitted light sought a decade earlier.

An affectionate, imaginative letter from his father: he imagines New York together again — the Empire State Building, Rockefeller Center, Radio City, the World's Fair the following summer, the Battery, the policeman pointing out the liners (Normandie at 4:30 p.m., Aquitania at 6 p.m., Queen Mary the following Tuesday), the aquarium, a hamburger with relish for the boy and onions and mustard for himself; he sends kisses to Cara, the mother, and the aunts, and shakes Essex's hand because he is a man. Normandie at 4:30 p.m., Aquitania at 6 p.m., Queen Mary on Tuesday; hamburger with relish / onions and mustard; the game “Wolf Kazan”

Albers makes tracings of Romanesque and Gothic architecture (including a side elevation of Cologne Cathedral) from Ernst Mossel's book “Vom Geheimnis der Form...” (1938), kept in a folder labeled “On Proportion”; they were therefore made after his arrival in America. folder “On Proportion”; Cologne Cathedral Consequences: continues the architectural explorations of his youth

In a 1938 campus bulletin, the weaving teacher Anni Albers urges her students and artists to practice free experimentation and to leave the safe ground of accepted conventions. Published in a campus bulletin, 1938. Consequences: An early illustration of the rhetoric of experimentation that structures the whole college.
Schawinsky's second original nonnarrative production at the college.

Schawinsky leaves the college; experimental theater will remain largely dormant there until The Ruse of Medusa in 1948. After BMC, he teaches at the New Bauhaus in Chicago and with Moholy-Nagy creates camouflage patterns for a U.S. Army project. Consequences: A theatrical tradition dormant for ten years

Schawinsky's production adapted from the Latin hymn Dies Irae on the Last Judgment: masks and costumes of abstract forms, dramatic spotlights and shadows, repetitive movements evoking funeral rites, theater in the round with spectators dressed in robes and masks seated in concentric circles around the central stage. Spectators costumed and masked, placed according to unconventional assignments; Schawinsky saw it as a revival of the medieval plays performed in the marketplace before the cathedral Consequences: A student actor killed himself; Schawinsky later distanced himself from the direct reenactment of the macabre material held responsible

She writes that life today is very bewildering, that nervous breakdowns are more frequent in our civilization, and that one must come down from the clouds to experience the most real thing there is: material.
Publishes “Work with Material” in Black Mountain College Bulletin 5, reprinted in College Art Journal in January 1944 Bulletin 5 of the college
Encouraged by his colleagues, Rice takes the first of several leaves
